title: Energy transfer and productivity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EC04a#t4 term and clue written for the game; EC04a#t2 term and clue written for the game; EC04a#t3 term and clue written for the game; EC04b#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EC04a#N.3, EC04b#N.7a, EC04a#N.5, EC04b#N.9, EC04a#N.12, EC04b#N.11, EC04b#N.15.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Food web
items.clue: Many linked feeding pathways in one community

items.label: Decomposers
items.clue: Organisms that feed on dead matter and respire, releasing heat

items.label: Trophic level
items.clue: A feeding position along a chain, numbered from 1 at the start

items.label: Net production
items.clue: The small part of a consumer's intake that becomes new biomass

questions.stem: What do the arrows in a food web represent?

options.text: The direction in which energy and biomass are transferred, from each organism to the organism that feeds on it.
The direction in which each consumer seeks its food, pointing from the feeder to the organism that it eats.
Every ecological interaction in the community, including competition between species that share a food source.
The route by which energy is returned from decomposers to producers so that it can pass around the community again.

questions.explanation: Arrows in food chains and food webs indicate the direction of transfer of energy and biomass, so they run from the food organism to the consumer.

questions.stem: A caterpillar ingests leaf material containing 100 kJ of energy. It egests 50 kJ in faeces, releases 35 kJ as heat through cell respiration and stores 15 kJ in new biomass. What happens to the energy in the faeces?

options.text: It is returned to the plant through the soil, so that the plant can use it again for growth instead of needing sunlight.
There is no usable energy in the faeces, because the 50 kJ was already released as heat inside the caterpillar's gut.
It passes to decomposers and detritus feeders, which release it as heat in respiration, not to the next trophic level.
It has been used up by the caterpillar and ceases to exist, since energy that is not stored as biomass is destroyed.

questions.stem: In a garden, blackbirds eat berries from shrubs and also eat snails, which feed on the leaves of the same shrubs. Which trophic level or levels does the blackbird occupy?

options.text: A primary consumer in the chain where it eats berries and a secondary consumer in the chain where it eats snails.
A secondary consumer only, because each species has a single trophic level that is fixed by its usual diet.
Secondary consumer in both chains, because a bird that eats animals is a carnivore and carnivores are secondary consumers.
Secondary consumer when eating berries and tertiary consumer when eating snails, since the shrub is the first consumer.

questions.stem: Why is much less energy available to the secondary consumers in a food chain than to the primary consumers?

options.text: Primary consumers use up most of their energy in moving and feeding, so that energy is destroyed and no longer exists.
Not all primary consumers are eaten, not all of what is eaten is absorbed, and most absorbed energy is released as heat in respiration.
Decomposers, which form the final trophic level, take the energy from primary consumers and return it to the producers.
Respiration in primary consumers captures all the released energy in ATP, and this ATP cannot be passed on to a predator.

questions.explanation: Uneaten organisms go to decomposers, undigested material is egested, and most absorbed energy is respired and lost as heat. Only energy in new biomass passes on.

questions.stem: In autumn, an oak tree drops its leaves. Over the next year, fungi and bacteria break the leaves down. What happens to the carbon and to the energy that were in the leaves?

options.text: Both return to the soil, where the oak's roots absorb them to grow new leaves next spring.
The carbon returns to the air as CO₂ and can be fixed again; the energy leaves as heat.
The energy goes back into the soil as nutrients, but the carbon stays locked in the soil for ever.
Both are destroyed as the leaves rot, so the ecosystem must replace them from outside.

questions.stem: In a classic study of the Silver Springs ecosystem in Florida, the energy flow through each trophic level (all in kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹) was: producers 20 810; primary consumers 3368; secondary consumers 383; tertiary consumers 21. What percentage of the energy at the primary consumer level was transferred to the secondary consumers?
questions.explanation: Energy at the higher level ÷ energy at the level below: 383 ÷ 3368 × 100 = 11.4%.

questions.stem: A wood mouse eats seeds containing 500 kJ of energy. 100 kJ is lost in faeces and urine, and 380 kJ is released in respiration. What percentage of the energy it ate is available to an owl that eats the mouse?
questions.explanation: 500 − (100 + 380) = 20 kJ; 20 ÷ 500 × 100 = 4%. The mouse is an endotherm: most of what it absorbs is respired, much of it to keep warm.
